query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting the heavy Hf component with a low‐density element such as Al in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy (e.g. targeting approximately a 50:50 ratio of Al to Hf) will reduce the overall density of the alloy without sacrificing its high strength at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and excellent compressive/tensile strength at both ambient and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace roughly half of the Hf content with aluminum to form an Al0.5Hf0.5MoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.conditions: Quasi‐static mechanical loading tests (compression and/or tension) conducted at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (around 1000 °C) in an inert environment to avoid oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: A single-phase (or near single-phase) solid-solution (BCC) microstructure with a homogeneous distribution of elements that benefits from both solid-solution and potential precipitation strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, with its low density, reduces the overall mass of the alloy while its incorporation in the BCC matrix induces additional lattice distortion. This can help maintain—or even slightly enhance—the solid solution strengthening. Controlled Al addition may also favor fine-scale precipitation or early ordering without destabilizing the phase, thereby preserving the high-temperature strength observed in the original alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a density reduction of roughly 15–20% relative to the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy while maintaining (within ±10%) similar yield strength, ductility, and work-hardening behavior at both room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: The mechanical properties and density of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy (~10.21 g/cm³, high yield strength at RT and ~1000 °C).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to as-cast refractory high-entropy alloys under quasi-static mechanical loading in inert atmospheres from ambient conditions to around 1000 °C; phase stability or microstructural changes beyond these conditions may not be addressed.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies (e.g., on Al-containing lightweight RHEAs and MD simulations adjusting Hf content in similar systems) support density reduction with minimal property loss, it is uncertain whether the substitution will prevent the formation of deleterious secondary phases at elevated temperatures. This extension combines insights from evidence showing that adding Al (or reducing high-density Hf) can lower density [PMC8746096::web::002::1_introduction] with observations that Hf content critically affects strength [PMC10254787::web::010::3_1_effects_of_hf_and_ta_contents]; the specific effect on a HfMoTaTiZr system remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the proposed Al0.5Hf0.5MoTaTiZr alloy using the same as-cast processing route as the original alloy. Characterize its phase structure via X-ray diffraction and microstructure via electron microscopy to ensure a solid-solution BCC structure. Perform quasi-static compression and/or tensile tests at room temperature and approximately 1000 °C. Measure the alloy’s density using appropriate methods (e.g., Archimedes’ method).
measurements: Phase structure and grain size (XRD, SEM/TEM)
Yield and ultimate strengths at RT and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-substituted alloy does not show at least a ~15% reduction in density compared to 10.21 g/cm³ (i.e. if density remains higher than approximately 8.7–9.0 g/cm³) or if its yield strength (and other key mechanical properties) deviates by more than ±10% from that of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr at both room temperature and 1000 °C, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloy (HEA) is a new type of multi-principal alloy material and the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr HEAs have attracted more and more attention from researchers due to their high melting point, special plasticity, and excellent corrosion resistance. In this paper, in order to reduce the density of the alloy and maintain the strength of the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr HEAs, the effects of high-density elements Hf and Ta on the properties of HEAs were explored for the first time based on molecular dynamics simulations. A low-density and high-strength Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr HEA suitable for laser melting deposition was designed and formed. Studies have shown that the decrease in the proportion of Ta element reduces the strength of HEA, while the decrease in Hf element increases the strength of HEA. The simultaneous decrease in the ratio of Hf and Ta elements reduces the elastic modulus and strength of HEA and leads to the coarsening of the alloy microstructure. The application of laser melting deposition (LMD) technology refines the grains and effectively solves the coarsening problem. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. Adding lightweight elements into RHEAs can effectively reduce the density and improve the specific strength [,,,]. For example, Senkov et al. fabricated Al0.4Hf0.6NbTaTiZr RHEA by adding Al into the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA. The density of the alloy decreased from 9.94 to 9.05 g/cm3, and the specific yield strength increased from 93.56 to 203.43 MPa∙cm3/g []. However, their plasticity deteriorated significantly. Recently, Yang et al. found that NbTiVTaAl0.25 RHEA with Al addition still have outstanding compressive plasticity greater than 50% []. Nevertheless, the specific strength of this alloy is only 151.48 MPa∙cm3/g, which has the potential for further improvement. In this work, a series of lightweight TaNbVTi-based RHEAs were fabricated by mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructural evolution and its effects on mechanical properties were analyzed.
